title: Standards and experimentation
bodyMd:
A fictional consortium of small instrument makers adopts a common connector specification. Before the standard, repairers often needed a different adapter for each maker’s devices. The consortium expects standardization to lower repair costs and make it easier for customers to combine products. Critics argue that a common specification will suppress experimentation by locking firms into one design.

An analyst distinguishes the interface from the functions behind it. A connector standard restricts how devices attach, but need not specify how a sensor measures a signal or how software processes it. By reducing the cost of making devices compatible, the standard might allow firms to experiment more extensively within those unrestricted components. Such a benefit is not automatic. If the interface cannot accommodate new data requirements, or if revising it requires unanimous agreement among firms with conflicting interests, it may eventually become a constraint on valuable innovations.

The analyst therefore recommends evaluating both the boundary chosen for standardization and the process for changing it. A narrow standard with a credible revision mechanism could support variety, whereas a broad, difficult-to-revise standard could impede it. This account does not resolve the consortium’s decision by classifying standardization as inherently favourable or unfavourable to innovation. Instead, it treats compatibility and experimentation as potentially complementary within an appropriately designed institutional arrangement. The relevant comparison is not between an imagined world without constraints and a constrained one: proprietary connectors already impose compatibility costs and may themselves restrict who can contribute new components.
